article_title: First Language and Second Language Writing: The Role of Linguistic Knowledge, Speed of Processing, and Metacognitive Knowledge
citation: R. Schoonen, A. van Gelderen, K. de Glopper, J. Hulstijn, A. Simis, P. Snellings, M. Stevenson. (2003). First language and second language writing: the role of linguistic knowledge, speed of processing, and metacognitive knowledge. Language Learning, 53(1), 165-202. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9922.00213
title: Component measures battery: linguistic knowledge, fluency, and metacognitive knowledge tests in L1 and L2
description: The study administered a battery of measures to 281 grade 8 students covering linguistic knowledge, speed of processing (fluency/accessibility), and metacognitive knowledge in both Dutch (L1) and English (L2), alongside writing performance tasks. These measures served as observed indicators in structural equation models estimating each component's contribution to writing. The battery enabled the cross-language comparison that showed fluency's added value was null once linguistic knowledge was accounted for.
requirements: Parallel measures in both L1 and L2
constraints: Measures designed for grade 8 students in the Dutch education context
target_learning_goals: Assessment of writing-related component skills in L1 and L2
examples: Used as indicators in SEM comparing component weights across languages
key_sources: R. Schoonen, A. van Gelderen, K. de Glopper, J. Hulstijn, A. Simis, P. Snellings, M. Stevenson. (2003). First language and second language writing: the role of linguistic knowledge, speed of processing, and metacognitive knowledge. Language Learning, 53(1), 165-202. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9922.00213

article_title: Didactic Model: Teaching the English Temporal System to Arabic Freshman Learners of English
citation: Hmidani, T. (2017). Didactic model: Teaching the English temporal system to Arabic freshman learners of English. Profile: Issues in Teachers' Professional Development, 19(Suppl. 1), 81-97. https://doi.org/10.15446/profile.v19n_sup1.68617
title: Use learners' L1 (colloquial Arabic) to make English tense distinctions explicit through translation exercises
description: The article recommends leveraging the learner's mother tongue to raise awareness of English tense distinctions that are not straightforwardly mapped from Modern Standard Arabic. Colloquial Arabic makes simple/progressive distinctions that MSA does not, and translation exercises show "how the English structure is rendered in Arabic". This principle is grounded in the study's finding that language awareness gains were the first and strongest outcome of the model.
requirements: Teacher competence to compare the L1 and L2 systems and support comprehension questions with Arabic when necessary
constraints: Tested with adult Arabic-speaking learners; the author notes more research is needed to see whether the approach can be adapted to students whose language background is not Arabic
target_learning_goals: language awareness of English tense and aspect distinctions
examples: The appendix asks students to translate sentences containing had + past participle into Modern Standard Arabic and to choose correct translations of underlined verbs according to context
key_sources: Hmidani, T. (2017). Didactic model: Teaching the English temporal system to Arabic freshman learners of English. Profile: Issues in Teachers' Professional Development, 19(Suppl. 1), 81-97. https://doi.org/10.15446/profile.v19n_sup1.68617

article_title: Language Choices of Language Teachers and Learners: Meta-Synthesis of Qualitative Research
citation: Yıldız, M. (2021). Language choices of language teachers and learners: Meta-synthesis of qualitative research. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 17(Special Issue 1), 472-492. https://www.jlls.org
title: Two-theme taxonomy of L1 stances in L2 classrooms: avoidance versus use
description: The article organizes the synthesized qualitative findings into two basic themes: "Avoidance of L1 in language classes" and "Use of L1 in language classes". The avoidance theme captures concerns that L1 overuse reduces target-language exposure and practice, while the use theme captures the varied purposes and amounts of L1 use reported by teachers and learners. This taxonomy is the article's top-level organizing framework, derived from coding 34 studies in NVivo through three-phase analysis.
requirements: Synthesis requires qualitative studies reporting participants' views or practices on L1 use obtained through interviews or observations
constraints: Based only on qualitative studies published 2010-2019 indexed in ERIC and Web of Science
target_learning_goals: informed language choice in L2 instruction
judicious L1 use for learning support
key_sources: Yıldız, M. (2021). Language choices of language teachers and learners: Meta-synthesis of qualitative research. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 17(Special Issue 1), 472-492. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1285162

article_title: Language Choices of Language Teachers and Learners: Meta-Synthesis of Qualitative Research
citation: Yıldız, M. (2021). Language choices of language teachers and learners: Meta-synthesis of qualitative research. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 17(Special Issue 1), 472-492. https://www.jlls.org
title: Three-function taxonomy of L1 use: academic, managerial, and socio-cultural functions
description: The article groups the purposes for which L1 is used or advocated in L2 classrooms into three themes: "academic functions", "managerial functions", and "socio-cultural functions". Academic functions include explaining aspects of the target language, facilitating and checking comprehension, translating, eliciting, and question-and-answer exchanges. Managerial functions include giving instructions, classroom management, feedback, and motivation. Socio-cultural functions include praising, joking, establishing rapport, and socialization. The taxonomy was derived from studies providing categories and classifications of L1 purposes.
requirements: Derived from qualitative studies reporting categories and classifications of L1 use purposes by teachers and students
constraints: Functions identified from studies of specific classroom contexts; the article notes L1 can serve various functions in a monolingual context but the target language seems obligatory in multilingual ones
target_learning_goals: understanding facilitative functions of L1 in L2 teaching
key_sources: Yıldız, M. (2021). Language choices of language teachers and learners: Meta-synthesis of qualitative research. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 17(Special Issue 1), 472-492. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1285162

article_title: Does Translation Contribute to Learners' Free Active Vocabulary?
citation: Asiyaban, A. & Bagheri, M. S. (2012). Does translation contribute to learners' free active vocabulary? Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 16(1), 111-121.
title: Use L1 translation deliberately in EFL vocabulary teaching to build free active vocabulary
description: The article recommends that teachers explicitly provide L1 equivalents of target words rather than avoiding the L1, arguing that translation "eases internalization of new words, decreases the time required for explanation of words, and provides learners with self-confidence." It presents translation as a legitimate, time-saving technique whose application benefits both teachers and students.
requirements: Teacher and learners share the same L1 (EFL context)
constraints: Findings contrast with approaches advocating minimal L1 use; the study tested only 20 concrete nouns with adult intermediate learners
examples: Experimental groups were taught twenty nouns via L1 translations over four sessions and outperformed groups taught with L2 definitions
key_sources: Asiyaban, A. & Bagheri, M. S. (2012). Does translation contribute to learners' free active vocabulary? Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 16(1), 111-121. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ979925
